###### Abstract

Self-evolving LLM agents promise to improve autonomously through
continual interaction and learning, reducing their dependence on
manually curated supervision. Realizing this promise requires not only
updating the agent, but also evolving its training experience as its
capabilities change. However, most existing pipelines rely on static
datasets or separately updated synthesis models, causing previously
useful tasks to become trivial while overly difficult tasks remain
uninformative. This growing mismatch between agent capability and
training experience limits sustained self-improvement. To address this
problem, we propose SynCo, an agentic data synthesis co-training
framework for self-evolving LLMs based on multi-agent reinforcement
learning. SynCo jointly optimizes two independently parameterized
agents: a Synthesizer that constructs training tasks from the Reasoner’s
evolving capability state, and a Reasoner that learns from the resulting
experience. Each synthesized task induces multiple Reasoner rollouts
whose outcomes provide complementary rewards to both agents. Correctness
feedback improves the Reasoner, while task quality, answer reliability,
and outcome-grounded teachability guide the Synthesizer. Their updates
are fed back into subsequent synthesis rounds, allowing the task-solving
policy and its training distribution to evolve together. Extensive
experiments across eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate
that SynCo substantially outperforms a broad range of existing
synthetic-data methods and controlled baselines, achieving the strongest
overall performance while deriving most of its gains from previously
unsolved problems.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model agents are increasingly expected to improve through
interaction and accumulated experience, rather than remain bounded by a
fixed collection of human-curated demonstrations ([Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1); [Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)). Yet most agent
training pipelines still rely on data that is static, externally
constructed, or only periodically refreshed. This creates a fundamental
mismatch: agent capabilities change throughout training, while the
distribution of learning experience does not ([Pahuja et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Liang et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)). Tasks that were once
informative may become trivial, whereas tasks far beyond the agent’s
competence continue to provide little useful learning signal. The
resulting misalignment between the learner and its data limits both
training efficiency and sustained improvement. A genuinely self-evolving
agent therefore requires not merely more synthetic data, but a source of
training experience that continuously adapts to its evolving
capabilities ([Cheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib6); [Yue et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)).

Recent work has begun to address this limitation through adaptive data
synthesis, weakness-driven task generation, and teacher–solver or
challenger–solver co-evolution ([Zhai et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Yang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9); [Yue et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)). These
approaches adapt the training data to the current learner by
regenerating, selecting, or reweighting tasks according to model
failures, uncertainty, or estimated difficulty. However, an adaptive
data distribution does not necessarily imply joint optimization of data
synthesis and task learning. Many existing frameworks still alternate
between generating tasks from a previous learner checkpoint and
subsequently training the learner on the resulting data ([Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10); [Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib11)). Although this
enables iterative adaptation, the synthesis policy and the task policy
are not optimized together from the same online interaction. Data
generation therefore remains an auxiliary process around agent training
rather than a learnable component of the training system itself. True
mutual evolution requires jointly optimizing the experience synthesizer
and the learner.

Such joint training creates a coupled and non-stationary learning
problem. The Synthesizer shapes the Reasoner’s optimization landscape
through the tasks it generates, while each Reasoner update redefines
which tasks remain useful. A task that is informative at one stage may
later become trivial, whereas a nominally difficult task may still
provide little supervision if the Reasoner consistently succeeds or
fails. The value of synthetic data therefore cannot be judged solely by
static properties such as validity, novelty, or nominal difficulty, but
must be grounded in the current Reasoner’s actual interaction with the
data ([Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9); [Kwan et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)).
This leads to the central question of our work: _Can agentic data
synthesis and task learning be formulated as a unified multi-agent
reinforcement learning process in which the data-synthesis policy and
the task-solving policy are jointly optimized and continuously evolve
together?_ Answering this question requires more than connecting a
generator to a learner. It requires a closed loop that integrates
learner-state observation, adaptive task generation, shared interaction
feedback, and online updates of both policies.

To address this challenge, we propose SynCo, an agentic data synthesis
co-training framework for self-evolving LLMs based on multi-agent
reinforcement learning. SynCo jointly optimizes two independently
parameterized agents: a _Synthesizer_ that constructs training tasks and
a _Reasoner_ that learns from them. At each iteration, the Synthesizer
observes an evolving context built from the recent synthetic data pool,
the Reasoner’s empirical capability profile, and feedback from rejected
tasks. It then generates a structured and verifiable task tailored to
the Reasoner’s current learning needs. The Reasoner performs multiple
solution rollouts, whose outcomes provide complementary learning signals
to both agents. Correctness rewards improve the Reasoner, while task
quality, answer reliability, and outcome-grounded teachability guide the
Synthesizer. Both policies are updated online through group-relative
policy optimization within the same multi-agent training process. Their
updates define the next synthesis round: the improved Reasoner induces a
new capability state, and the improved Synthesizer converts that state
into a new training distribution. Through this closed loop, SynCo
enables the task-solving policy and its training data to evolve
together.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We formulate agentic data synthesis and task learning as a coupled
  multi-agent reinforcement learning problem, and propose SynCo to
  jointly optimize a Synthesizer and a Reasoner within a unified online
  training process.
- •
  We develop a closed-loop self-evolution framework in which the
  Synthesizer continually adapts the training distribution to the
  evolving Reasoner, while outcome-grounded interaction feedback from
  the Reasoner directly supervises the synthesis policy.
- •
  Extensive experiments across diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks
  show that SynCo consistently outperforms a frozen-Synthesizer
  baseline, with most gains arising from previously unsolved problems.

## 2 Related Work

Synthetic data has become central to LLM post-training, ranging from
instruction bootstrapping methods such as Self-Instruct ([Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib13)) and WizardLM ([Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)) to
reasoning-oriented pipelines such as STaR ([Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib15)), MetaMath ([Yu et al., 2023](#bib.bib16)), and
DeepSeekMath ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)). Recent work further
improves realism, diversity, verifiability, and learner relevance:
MATRIX ([Tang et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) generates scenarios through
multi-agent simulation, FAC Synthesis ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18))
targets missing representation-space features, Explorer ([Pahuja et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3)) synthesizes trajectories through environment
exploration, and SwS ([Liang et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)) constructs
problems around persistent learner weaknesses. Related pipelines extend
synthetic supervision to mathematical reasoning, tool use, web
interaction, and executable environments ([Gou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19); [Ramrakhya et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib21); [Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib22)). Most of these
approaches nevertheless construct an offline corpus or adapt generation
separately from downstream policy optimization.

Self-evolving frameworks more directly couple experience generation with
learner improvement. R-Zero ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)),
Socratic-Zero ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib11)), and Agent0 ([Xia
et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)) establish co-evolving proposer, teacher, or
curriculum roles for autonomous reasoning improvement. Dr. Zero ([Yue
et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)) and SCOPE ([Kwan et al., 2026](#bib.bib12))
extend this paradigm to multi-turn search and open-ended
document-grounded tasks, while CoEvolve ([Yang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib9)) adapts tool-use task distributions using
rollout-derived forgetting and uncertainty signals. Agent-World ([Dong
et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)), SEAD ([Dai et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)),
AgentEvolver ([Zhai et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)), EvolveR ([Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib26)), and EvoFSM ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib6))
further explore the evolution of environments, curricula, memories,
experiences, and agent workflows. A comprehensive discussion of
synthetic-data generation and self-evolving agents is provided in
Appendix.A.

## 3 Method

In this section, we present SynCo, a multi-agent reinforcement learning
framework that jointly optimizes agentic data synthesis and task
reasoning for continual self-evolution. The overall framework is
illustrated in
Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Method ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning").

![Refer to caption](2610.11345v1/Picture1.png)

Figure 1: Overview of SynCo, a closed-loop framework for self-evolving
LLMs. (1) A Synthesizer first generates capability-guided and verifiable
tasks from the current learning context. (2) The resulting interaction
batch is then used to jointly update the Synthesizer and the Reasoner
through online multi-agent co-training. (3) The updated agents in turn
reshape the future curriculum and task distribution, forming an
agent–data self-evolution loop.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation: Agentic Data Synthesis Co-Training

We consider two independently parameterized agents: a _Synthesizer_
$`\pi_{S}(\cdot;\theta_{S})`$ that generates training tasks and a
_Reasoner_ $`\pi_{R}(\cdot;\theta_{R})`$ that learns to solve them. The
Synthesizer determines the Reasoner’s training experience, while the
Reasoner’s realized behavior provides feedback for improving synthesis.

At iteration $`t`$, a dynamic context $`c_{t}`$ summarizes the
Reasoner’s recent capabilities, the coverage of previously generated
tasks, and feedback from rejected samples. Conditioned on $`c_{t}`$, the
Synthesizer generates a structured and verifiable task:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
x_{t}\sim\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid c_{t};\theta_{S}^{t}),\qquad\mathcal{D}_{t}=\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid c_{t};\theta_{S}^{t}),
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ is the online training distribution induced by
the current learner state and synthesis policy.

For each admitted task $`x_{t}`$ with verified answer $`a_{t}^{\star}`$,
the Reasoner samples $`K`$ independent rollouts
$`y_{t}^{(k)}\sim\pi_{R}(\cdot\mid x_{t};\theta_{R}^{t})`$, whose
outcomes are determined by
$`z_{t}^{(k)}=\operatorname{Check}(y_{t}^{(k)},a_{t}^{\star})`$. The
same interaction yields rollout-level correctness rewards
$`r_{R,t}^{(k)}`$ for the Reasoner and a task-level reward $`r_{S,t}`$
that evaluates both synthesis quality and realized utility for the
current Reasoner.

The agents optimize distinct but coupled objectives:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J_{R}(\theta_{R})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_{R,t}^{(k)}\right],\qquad J_{S}(\theta_{S})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[r_{S,t}\right].
``` |  | (2) |

The objectives are coupled because $`\pi_{S}`$ determines the
distribution underlying $`J_{R}`$, whereas $`\pi_{R}`$ produces the
interaction feedback underlying $`J_{S}`$. Both policies are updated
from the same online batch using agent-specific group-relative policy
optimization, forming a unified co-training process rather than
sequential synthesis and learning.

### 3.2 Capability-Conditioned Agentic Data Synthesis

A self-evolving Reasoner requires training experience that remains
aligned with its changing capabilities. Rather than sampling from a
fixed generator, the Synthesizer observes recent agent–data
interactions, identifies which capabilities should be exercised next,
and realizes this decision as a structured and verifiable task. Data
generation therefore becomes an adaptive policy conditioned on the
evolving learner.

#### Capability-conditioned synthesis context.

Let $`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$ denote the interaction memory before iteration
$`t`$, containing recent tasks, validation outcomes, Reasoner rollouts
and success rates, synthesis rewards, and rejection records. We
summarize it as

|     |                                                          |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       c_{t}=G(\mathcal{M}_{t})=\left(p_{t},d_{t},e_{t}\right),
       ```                                                       |     | (3) |

where $`p_{t}`$ characterizes the current synthetic pool and its
coverage, $`d_{t}`$ summarizes the Reasoner’s empirical performance and
remaining weaknesses, and $`e_{t}`$ records synthesis failures,
redundancy, and under-explored task regions. The context is
reconstructed throughout training, allowing synthesis to adapt as both
the Reasoner and the accumulated task distribution evolve.

#### Structured pedagogical task generation.

Conditioned on $`c_{t}`$, the Synthesizer generates a structured task
card

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
x_{t}=\left(q_{t},\mathbf{m}_{t},s_{t}^{\star},a_{t}^{\star}\right)\sim\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid c_{t};\theta_{S}^{t}),
``` |  | (4) |

where $`q_{t}`$ is the problem presented to the Reasoner,
$`\mathbf{m}_{t}`$ specifies its pedagogical intent and estimated
difficulty, and $`(s_{t}^{\star},a_{t}^{\star})`$ provides a reference
solution and final answer for verification. The metadata encourages an
explicit synthesis decision by specifying the targeted reasoning
behavior, anticipated weakness, and novelty or verification
requirements. Accordingly, the Synthesizer is instructed to produce
tasks that are original, self-contained, non-trivial, and aligned with
weaknesses or under-explored capabilities identified in $`c_{t}`$.

The reference solution, answer, and metadata are used only for
validation and reward computation. The Reasoner receives $`q_{t}`$
alone, preventing answer leakage and ensuring that its rollout outcomes
reflect its own policy.

#### Verified admission.

Because open-ended generation may produce malformed, ambiguous,
inconsistent, or repetitive tasks, every task is evaluated by a verifier
$`V(x_{t})=(v_{t},\boldsymbol{\rho}_{t})`$. Here,
$`\boldsymbol{\rho}_{t}`$ records schema validity, problem completeness,
answer consistency, output format, and duplication, while $`v_{t}`$
determines whether the task enters Reasoner training:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
v_{t}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[x_{t}\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{valid}}\right],\ \widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{t}=\left\{x_{t}\sim\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid c_{t};\theta_{S}^{t})\mid v_{t}=1\right\}.
``` |  | (5) |

When enabled, an additional consensus check independently solves the
generated problem and rejects tasks whose inferred answers do not
support the Synthesizer-provided reference. Invalid tasks are excluded
from Reasoner training and return negative feedback to the Synthesizer,
whereas admitted tasks form the adaptive distribution used for
subsequent multi-agent optimization.

### 3.3 Interaction-Grounded Multi-Agent Co-Training

The verified tasks provide a shared interaction space for both agents.
For each admitted task, the Reasoner’s rollouts simultaneously provide
direct supervision for task solving and outcome-grounded feedback for
data synthesis. This shared interaction couples the two policies within
the same online training process.

#### Reasoner interaction and outcome verification.

Given a valid task $`x_{t}`$, the Reasoner receives only its problem
statement $`q_{t}`$ and samples $`K`$ independent trajectories:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle y_{t}^{(k)}`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim\pi_{R}(\cdot\mid q_{t};\theta_{R}^{t}),`$ |  | (6) |
|  | $`\displaystyle z_{t}^{(k)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{Check}\left(\hat{a}_{t}^{(k)},a_{t}^{\star}\right)\in\{0,1\},`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mu_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}z_{t}^{(k)},\qquad k=1,\ldots,K,`$ |  |  |

where $`\hat{a}_{t}^{(k)}`$ is the extracted answer and $`\mu_{t}`$ is
the empirical success rate of the current Reasoner on task $`x_{t}`$.
The checker supports normalized exact, numerical, symbolic, and set- or
tuple-level equivalence. The resulting rollout group distinguishes
uniformly solved or failed tasks from those producing mixed outcomes,
making $`\mu_{t}`$ an outcome-grounded measure of task utility for the
current Reasoner.

#### Agent-specific interaction rewards.

The Reasoner is optimized with rollout-level correctness rewards,
encouraging trajectories that produce verified answers. The Synthesizer
instead receives a task-level gated reward:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{S,t}=G_{q}\!\left(r_{t}^{\mathrm{quality}}\right)G_{r}\!\left(r_{t}^{\mathrm{reliability}}\right)T(\mu_{t}),
``` |  | (7) |

where $`G_{q}`$ and $`G_{r}`$ softly gate task quality and answer
reliability, while $`T(\mu_{t})`$ measures realized teachability from
the Reasoner’s rollout outcomes. The teachability signal is maximized
for tasks producing mixed success and decreases toward uniformly solved
or failed tasks, which provide little group-relative learning signal.
Thus, quality and reliability constrain the feasible synthesis space,
while the current Reasoner’s behavior determines which valid tasks are
most useful for learning. Exact reward definitions and implementation
constants are provided in
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Reward and Verification Details ‣ Appendix B Method ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning").

#### Joint multi-agent update.

At each iteration, the system collects a shared online interaction batch

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{B}_{t}=\left\{\left(c_{i},\,x_{i},\,\left\{y_{i}^{(k)},z_{i}^{(k)}\right\}_{k=1}^{K}\right)\right\}_{i=1}^{B}.
``` |  | (8) |

The same interaction batch induces separate group-relative objectives
for the two agents: rollout-level correctness optimizes the Reasoner,
while gated task utility optimizes the Synthesizer. Although their
parameters and rewards remain separate, both policies are updated within
the same training iteration:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{R}^{t+1}=\theta_{R}^{t}-\eta_{R}\nabla_{\theta_{R}}\mathcal{L}_{R}^{t},\qquad\theta_{S}^{t+1}=\theta_{S}^{t}-\eta_{S}\nabla_{\theta_{S}}\mathcal{L}_{S}^{t}.
``` |  | (9) |

The Synthesizer determines the task distribution from which the Reasoner
learns, while the Reasoner’s realized outcomes determine the learning
signal for the Synthesizer. Updating either policy therefore changes the
other’s subsequent learning problem, forming a coupled online
co-training process.

### 3.4 Closed-Loop Agent–Data Self-Evolution

The co-training procedure in
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Interaction-Grounded Multi-Agent Co-Training ‣ 3 Method ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
updates both the Reasoner and the policy that generates its training
experience. To sustain self-evolution, each interaction batch is fed
back into a persistent memory that reconstructs the learner state and
conditions the next synthesis round.

#### Feedback-driven context renewal.

After processing $`\mathcal{B}_{t}`$, the system records the generated
tasks, validation results, verified rollouts, empirical success rates,
and agent-specific rewards. Rejected tasks and their failure reasons are
also retained to discourage repeated malformed, unreliable, or redundant
generations. The memory and synthesis context are updated as

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{t+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{Update}\left(\mathcal{M}_{t},\mathcal{B}_{t}\right),`$ |  | (10) |
|  | $`\displaystyle c_{t+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=G\!\left(\operatorname{Recent}\left(\mathcal{M}_{t+1}\right)\right).`$ |  |  |

The recent interaction window emphasizes the Reasoner’s current behavior
while retaining sufficient history to summarize task coverage, recurring
weaknesses, and synthesis failures. Thus, the synthesis condition
evolves from realized learning behavior: previously challenging tasks
may become trivial, new weaknesses may emerge, and over-produced
reasoning patterns may be suppressed.

#### Coupled evolution of agents and data.

As the Reasoner changes, the utility of a task becomes non-stationary:
$`\mu(x;\pi_{R}^{t+1})\neq\mu(x;\pi_{R}^{t})`$. A task that once
produced mixed outcomes may later become uniformly solvable, while
another may enter the learnable region as prerequisite capabilities
improve. Meanwhile, the updated Synthesizer changes how the renewed
learner state is translated into future tasks. The next verified
distribution is therefore

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{t+1}=\left\{x\sim\pi_{S}\left(\cdot\mid c_{t+1};\theta_{S}^{t+1}\right)\;\middle|\;V(x).v=1\right\}.
``` |  | (11) |

Compared with $`\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{t}`$, this distribution changes
through both a renewed context and an updated synthesis policy. SynCo
therefore does not merely query a fixed generator with a revised prompt;
it jointly adapts the state conditioning generation and the policy that
performs it.

## 4 Experiments

Benchmarks. We evaluate mathematical reasoning on eight benchmarks:
GSM8K, SVAMP, ASDiv, GSM-Hard, MATH-500, AIME24, AIME25, and Minerva,
reporting answer accuracy under a unified verification protocol.
Baselines. We compare SynCo against existing synthetic-data methods,
including AgenticQwen, EnvScaler, AgentSkiller, Klear-AgentForge,
MetaMathQA, ScaleQuest-Math, OpenMathInstruct-2, and R-Zero, together
with three controlled alternatives: Static-Pool GRPO, Offline-Augment
GRPO, and Reject-Sample SFT. We additionally include SynCo (Frozen
Synth), which retains learner-conditioned online synthesis but disables
Synthesizer updates. Implementation Details. We use Qwen3-8B as the
default backbone and additionally evaluate Qwen3-4B for cross-scale
validation. Training is implemented with the UnityMAS-O multi-agent RL
framework using GRPO. Complete benchmark descriptions, training
configurations, synthesis prompts, hyperparameters, and evaluation
details are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.1 RQ1: Does Co-Training Data Synthesis Improve Reasoning Performance?

Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Coupled evolution of agents and data. ‣ 3.4 Closed-Loop Agent–Data Self-Evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
presents the overall reasoning performance across eight mathematical
benchmarks. Across the broader comparison, existing synthetic-data
methods achieve substantially lower average performance than SynCo;
among them, ScaleQuest-Math is the strongest with 74.96%, while the
controlled Static-Pool GRPO, Reject-Sample SFT, and Offline-Augment GRPO
baselines reach 71.75%, 72.23%, and 73.13%, respectively. The
frozen-Synthesizer baseline improves further to 75.85%, whereas SynCo
reaches 78.72%, outperforming the strongest external baseline by 3.76
percentage points, Frozen by 2.87 points, and Vanilla by 6.36 points.
SynCo achieves the best or tied-best result on six of the eight
benchmarks and ranks second on the remaining two, indicating
substantially more consistent improvements than methods that peak on
individual datasets. Relative to Frozen, the gains include 2.20 points
on MATH-500, 2.05 points on GSM-Hard, and 1.67 points on SVAMP, while
ASDiv is already near saturation. On the advanced benchmarks, SynCo
improves AIME24 and AIME25 by 6.66 points each and Minerva by 2.57
points over Frozen. The overall results show that jointly adapting the
synthesis policy yields a stronger and more broadly effective training
distribution than existing synthetic-data approaches or a frozen
Synthesizer. The same pattern is reproduced with Qwen3-4B, where
co-training yields consistent improvements over the frozen variant, as
reported in
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Generalization Across Model Scales ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.2 RQ2: How Does the Synthesized Curriculum Evolve During Co-Training?

![Refer to
caption](2610.11345v1/figures2/exp2_synthesizer_evolution.png)

Figure 2: Evolution of the synthesized curriculum during co-training.
Tasks are ordered by generation time and divided into ten equally sized
buckets. (a) Realized Reasoner outcomes, where gradient-bearing tasks
have non-identical rollout rewards (equivalently, $`0<SR<1`$ under our
reward setting). (b) Evolution of synthesis signals, showing that task
quality and novelty remain high while realized teachability declines.
Generation order approximates training progression because exact
iteration indices were not recorded.

Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 RQ2: How Does the Synthesized Curriculum Evolve During Co-Training? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
reveals a progressive shift in the utility of the synthesized
curriculum. From the first to the final bucket, the proportion of
gradient-bearing tasks decreases from 31.3% to 9.5%, while the
all-correct proportion increases from 34.4% to 59.9%, indicating that an
increasing fraction of generated tasks becomes uniformly solvable as the
Reasoner improves. Meanwhile, task quality remains consistently high and
novelty increases from 0.659 to 0.775, whereas teachability declines
sharply from 0.206 to 0.060. The full-pool statistics in Appendix
D.Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.2 How Does the Synthesized Curriculum Evolve During Co-Training? ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
further show that only 16.2% of the 2,940 verified tasks provide
non-degenerate group-relative feedback, and that teachability strongly
tracks this gradient-bearing property ($`r=0.934`$), unlike novelty
($`r=-0.041`$). These results distinguish task validity and diversity
from realized optimization utility: well-formed and novel tasks may
still provide no effective policy gradient for the current Reasoner.
Thus, although SynCo achieves consistent downstream gains, maintaining
an informative curriculum becomes increasingly difficult as the learner
evolves, motivating synthesis objectives grounded directly in realized
rollout outcomes. Additional analyses are in Appendix.D.

### 4.3 RQ3: Where Do the Gains from Co-Training Arise?

To distinguish capability acquisition from preservation of existing
knowledge, we partition each benchmark according to the initial Qwen3-8B
predictions. As shown in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 RQ3: Where Do the Gains from Co-Training Arise? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning"),
SynCo and SynCo (Frozen Synth.) remain nearly identical on the Retain
subset, whereas a much larger gap emerges on examples that the initial
model fails to solve. In the pooled results, the Learn subset improves
from 27.11% to 32.23%, while the Retain subset changes only from 98.52%
to 98.95%. Correspondingly, 45 of the 56 additional solved examples
arise from the Learn subset, showing that the advantage of co-training
is dominated by capability acquisition rather than improved preservation
of already mastered behavior. This pattern is consistent across all four
benchmarks, indicating that adapting the synthesis policy does not
merely reinforce the current policy but reallocates training experience
toward regions where unresolved yet learnable problems remain. Together
with the curriculum analysis in
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 RQ2: How Does the Synthesized Curriculum Evolve During Co-Training? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning"),
these results suggest that learner-adaptive synthesis is particularly
valuable near the evolving capability frontier, where informative
training experience can be converted into new problem-solving
competence. A complete benchmark-level decomposition is provided in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Attributing Gains to Capability Acquisition ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
and
Figure [7](#A4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ D.3 Attributing Gains to Capability Acquisition ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.4 RQ4: Which Synthesis Signals Align with Gradient-Bearing Tasks?

![Refer to caption](2610.11345v1/figures2/exp4_reward_enrichment.png)

Figure 3: Counterfactual enrichment analysis of synthesis signals. Tasks
are reranked offline using different signals, and the proportion of
gradient-bearing tasks in the top-ranked quartile is reported.
Outcome-grounded teachability strongly enriches for gradient-bearing
tasks, whereas static task-level signals provide substantially weaker
separation.

Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 RQ4: Which Synthesis Signals Align with Gradient-Bearing Tasks? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
shows that outcome-grounded teachability is the synthesis signal most
strongly aligned with optimization utility. Relative to the 16.2%
gradient-bearing prevalence in the full task pool, ranking by the SynCo
gated reward increases this proportion to 62.3%, while teachability
alone reaches 64.6%. In contrast, quality and novelty alone yield only
12.8% and 12.0%, respectively, both below the pool prevalence. The
signal-level statistics in
Table [6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ D.4 Synthesis Signals and Realized Gradient Utility ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
further show that teachability strongly correlates with the
gradient-bearing indicator ($`r=0.934`$), whereas static task-level
signals exhibit weak alignment. These results separate task feasibility
from learning utility: quality and reliability help ensure trustworthy
tasks, but the Reasoner’s realized rollout outcomes determine whether a
task provides informative group-relative feedback. The gated reward
therefore preserves the strong outcome signal while constraining
optimization to valid and reliable tasks, supporting the central design
of SynCo. Because this analysis reranks an already collected task pool,
it should be interpreted as a diagnostic analysis rather than a causal
training ablation; additional results are provided in
Appendix [D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Synthesis Signals and Realized Gradient Utility ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.5 RQ5: Can the Synthesizer Anticipate Gradient Utility Before Rollout?

![Refer to
caption](2610.11345v1/figures2/exp5_difficulty_calibration.png)

Figure 4: Realized Reasoner outcomes under the Synthesizer’s ex-ante
difficulty estimates. Harder labels shift tasks from uniformly correct
toward uniformly incorrect outcomes, indicating coarse difficulty
awareness. However, the gradient-bearing proportion remains nearly
unchanged across difficulty categories, showing that nominal difficulty
does not predict realized optimization utility.

Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.5 RQ5: Can the Synthesizer Anticipate Gradient Utility Before Rollout? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
shows that the Synthesizer’s ex-ante estimates capture coarse task
difficulty but fail to identify tasks with useful realized learning
signal. As the label shifts from *learnable* to *hard/too hard*, the
all-correct rate decreases from 53.0% to 39.9%, while the all-incorrect
rate increases from 30.2% to 44.1%. However, this shift occurs almost
entirely between the two zero-gradient extremes: the gradient-bearing
rate remains nearly constant at 16.8%, 16.0%, and 16.0% across the three
major difficulty groups, closely matching the 16.2% pool prevalence.
Table [7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ D.4 Synthesis Signals and Realized Gradient Utility ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
further shows that treating the *learnable* label as a predictor yields
only $`r=0.009`$, 16.8% precision, and 22.3% recall. In contrast, the
ex-post teachability signal studied in
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 RQ4: Which Synthesis Signals Align with Gradient-Bearing Tasks? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
reaches $`r=0.934`$ after observing the Reasoner’s rollouts. Thus, the
Synthesizer can broadly anticipate whether tasks will be easier or
harder, but cannot reliably identify the intermediate region that
produces non-degenerate learning signals. This gap shows that nominal
difficulty alone cannot substitute for learner interaction, supporting
the outcome-grounded feedback design of SynCo. Additional calibration
results are provided in
Appendix [D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Why Ex-Ante Difficulty Does Not Predict Gradient Utility ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.6 RQ6: How Efficient Is Online Synthesizer–Reasoner Co-Training?

|------------|------------|------------|-------------|-------------|
| Variant    | Update     | Wall       | Grad. Rate  | Tasks/Batch |
| Frozen     | 45.8 s     | 341.6 s    | 13.7%       | 4.38        |
| SynCo      | 45.1 s     | 343.5 s    | 14.5%       | 4.64        |
| $`\Delta`$ | $`-1.5\%`$ | $`+0.6\%`$ | $`+0.8`$ pp | $`+0.26`$   |

Table 3: Training cost and gradient utilization for Frozen Synthesizer
and SynCo. Times are measured per training step, and productive rate
denotes the fraction of gradient-bearing tasks.

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.6 RQ6: How Efficient Is Online Synthesizer–Reasoner Co-Training? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
shows that jointly optimizing the Synthesizer introduces negligible
marginal overhead relative to the matched frozen-Synthesizer pipeline.
The mean update time remains essentially unchanged (45.1 s vs. 45.8 s),
while median end-to-end time differs by only 0.6%. Under this comparable
cost, SynCo increases the productive-task rate from 13.7% to 14.5%,
corresponding to 4.64 versus 4.38 productive tasks per batch. This
indicates that the benefit of co-training comes from reallocating the
training distribution toward more informative interactions rather than
simply increasing computation or rollout volume. Because both variants
share the same Reasoner optimization budget and per-task rollout
configuration, the comparison isolates the effect of adapting the
synthesis policy itself. The higher productive-task rate further
suggests that this adaptation improves how efficiently the fixed
interaction budget is converted into useful learning signal. Thus, the
gains from co-training are not explained by additional per-step
computation, but by a more effective online training distribution.
Complete timing and data-production statistics are provided in
Appendix [D.6](#A4.SS6 "D.6 Training Efficiency, Gradient Utilization, and Data Production ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.7 RQ7: Does SynCo Better Match the Learner’s Capability Boundary?

![Refer to caption](2610.11345v1/figures2/fig_boundary_utility.png)

Figure 5: Learner-relative comparison of synthetic data from SynCo,
MetaMathQA, ScaleQuest-Math, and OpenMathInstruct-2 under the same
Vanilla Qwen3-8B Reasoner and rollout protocol. (a) Distribution of
realized rollout outcomes, highlighting the proportion of
gradient-bearing tasks. (b) Full Reasoner success-rate distribution,
showing how each data source is positioned relative to the learner’s
capability boundary.

![Refer to
caption](2610.11345v1/figures2/reasoner_reward_comparison.png)

Figure 6: Reasoner reward trajectories under a frozen Synthesizer and
joint Synthesizer–Reasoner co-training. Curves report 10-step moving
averages. After comparable early progress, SynCo maintains a
consistently higher reward trajectory.

Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.7 RQ7: Does SynCo Better Match the Learner’s Capability Boundary? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
compares the learner-relative utility of SynCo data with three
representative static synthetic-data sources under the same Vanilla
Qwen3-8B Reasoner, rollout budget, and answer checker. SynCo places
22.8% of its tasks in the gradient-bearing region, compared with 4.1%
for MetaMathQA, 10.9% for ScaleQuest-Math, and 9.4% for
OpenMathInstruct-2, corresponding to a $`2.1`$–$`5.5\times`$ increase in
potentially informative group-relative interactions. Panel (b) further
shows that this advantage does not arise simply from generating harder
problems: MetaMathQA is overwhelmingly concentrated at
$`\mathrm{SR}=1`$, whereas OpenMathInstruct-2 places substantially more
mass at $`\mathrm{SR}=0`$, and both therefore contain relatively few
intermediate-outcome tasks. In contrast, SynCo distributes considerably
more probability mass across $`\mathrm{SR}\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}`$,
indicating stronger concentration near the current learner’s capability
boundary. These results provide a data-side explanation for the
downstream gains in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 RQ1: Does Co-Training Data Synthesis Improve Reasoning Performance? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning"):
the benefit of learner-conditioned synthesis is not merely producing
difficult or diverse problems, but generating more training experiences
that are appropriately matched to the current Reasoner and yield
non-degenerate learning signal.

### 4.8 RQ8: How Does Co-Training Affect the Reasoner’s Optimization Dynamics?

Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.7 RQ7: Does SynCo Better Match the Learner’s Capability Boundary? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
compares the Reasoner’s optimization trajectories under the two training
regimes. Both variants improve rapidly at the beginning, indicating that
online synthesized tasks already provide useful training signal with a
frozen Synthesizer. The trajectories begin to separate after
approximately 35 steps, after which SynCo maintains a consistently
higher moving-average reward. By the end of training, SynCo reaches
0.890 compared with 0.783 for the frozen-Synthesizer baseline. This
sustained divergence shows that the benefit of co-training emerges
progressively as the synthesis policy adapts to the evolving Reasoner,
rather than only appearing at a particular evaluation checkpoint.
Together with the downstream gains in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 RQ1: Does Co-Training Data Synthesis Improve Reasoning Performance? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning"),
these dynamics provide process-level evidence that joint
Synthesizer–Reasoner optimization produces a more effective training
trajectory.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced SynCo, a multi-agent framework that jointly
optimizes task synthesis and reasoning through shared online
interaction. Across eight mathematical benchmarks, SynCo consistently
improves over a frozen Synthesizer, with gains primarily arising from
previously unsolved problems. Our analyses further show that static task
properties such as quality or novelty are insufficient to identify
useful training experience, whereas outcome-grounded teachability is
strongly aligned with gradient-bearing interactions throughout training.
Co-training achieves these gains with little measurable marginal
overhead, establishing adaptive data synthesis as a learnable and
scalable component of self-evolving LLM training.

## Appendix

## Appendix A Related Work

Large language models have increasingly been extended into autonomous
agents capable of planning, tool use, memory, and multi-step interaction
with external environments \[[Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib27), [Guo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib28), [Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib29), [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib30), [Ping et al., 2025](#bib.bib31), [Qin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32), [Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib33), [Yang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib34)\]. Building on these capabilities, multi-agent
systems coordinate multiple specialized agents through communication,
collaboration, and iterative feedback, and have been explored across
reasoning, coding, web interaction, and other complex decision-making
tasks \[[Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib35), [He et al., 2024](#bib.bib36),
[Chang et al., 2025](#bib.bib37), [Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib38), [Yang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib39), [Yang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib40), [Chen
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib41), [Ping et al., 2026](#bib.bib42), [Yang
et al., 2026e](#bib.bib43)\]. These developments motivate learning
frameworks in which agents not only solve tasks, but also actively
construct and adapt the experience used for subsequent training.

### A.1 Synthetic Data for LLM Post-Training

Synthetic data has become an important source of supervision for
post-training large language models \[[Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)\].
Early instruction-synthesis methods, including Self-Instruct \[[Wang
et al., 2023](#bib.bib13)\], WizardLM \[[Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)\],
and instruction backtranslation \[[Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib44)\],
bootstrap instruction–response pairs from seed demonstrations, teacher
models, or unlabeled corpora. Subsequent work improves the realism,
diversity, and coverage of generated data. MATRIX \[[Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)\] constructs realistic post-training scenarios through
multi-agent simulation, while FAC Synthesis \[[Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib18)\] explicitly targets missing features in the model’s
representation space. Other approaches employ iterative refinement,
filtering, and autonomous data engineering to better align synthetic
corpora with downstream learning objectives \[[Cao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib45), [Tu et al., 2025](#bib.bib46)\]. These studies
establish data generation as an important dimension of LLM
post-training, but typically construct an offline corpus that is
subsequently consumed by a separately optimized learner.

Reasoning-oriented synthesis places additional emphasis on solution
quality and answer verifiability. STaR \[[Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib15)\] bootstraps reasoning traces from successful model
generations, while WizardMath \[[Luo et al., 2025](#bib.bib47)\] and
MetaMath \[[Yu et al., 2023](#bib.bib16)\] expand mathematical
supervision through instruction evolution and multi-perspective problem
augmentation. MAmmoTH \[[Yue et al., 2024](#bib.bib48)\] combines
natural-language and program-based rationales, whereas ToRA \[[Gou
et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)\] constructs tool-integrated reasoning
trajectories. DeepSeekMath \[[Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)\],
NuminaMath \[[Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib49)\], and related mathematical
post-training pipelines further demonstrate the effectiveness of
large-scale curated or synthesized reasoning corpora paired with outcome
verification. More recently, SwS \[[Liang et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)\]
identifies persistent learner weaknesses and synthesizes new problems
targeting the corresponding concepts. Together with reinforcement
learning from verifiable rewards, these methods enable scalable
reasoning supervision without requiring process-level human preference
annotations.

Synthetic experience has also become central to training tool-using and
interactive agents. Explorer \[[Pahuja et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)\]
synthesizes diverse multimodal web trajectories through large-scale
environment exploration, while OS-Genesis \[[Sun et al.,
2025](#bib.bib50)\] derives executable GUI tasks from successful
interaction trajectories. AutoPlay \[[Ramrakhya et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20)\] explores application states before generating
environment-grounded tasks; Trajectory2Task \[[Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib21)\] transforms valid tool trajectories into verifiable
user-facing tasks; and WebAggregator \[[Wang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib51)\] constructs search tasks requiring compositional
evidence aggregation. EigenData \[[Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib22)\]
synthesizes multi-turn tool-use dialogues together with executable
checkers, whereas DreamGym \[[Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)\] uses a
learned experience model to scale synthetic tasks and interactions.
These pipelines improve feasibility, environmental grounding, diversity,
and verifiability, but their generators are commonly fixed,
prompt-optimized, or updated separately from the policy trained on the
resulting experience.

In group-relative reinforcement learning, however, the value of a task
is not determined by validity, novelty, or nominal difficulty alone.
Even a well-formed task provides no discriminative policy signal when
all sampled solutions are correct or all are incorrect, and its learning
utility changes as the Reasoner evolves. SynCo therefore formulates data
synthesis as a trainable policy conditioned on the current learner
state. By optimizing the Synthesizer through verified downstream
interaction, the training distribution can evolve according to the
realized teachability of generated tasks rather than only their static
data properties.

### A.2 Self-Evolving LLMs and Agent–Data Co-Training

Self-evolving LLMs seek to reduce dependence on externally constructed
supervision by generating and learning from their own
experience \[[Cheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)\]. R-Zero \[[Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)\] initializes independently parameterized Challenger
and Solver policies that co-evolve through task generation and solution
feedback. Socratic-Zero \[[Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib11)\] extends
this paradigm with Teacher, Solver, and Generator roles, using diagnosed
learner weaknesses to construct an increasingly challenging mathematical
curriculum. Agent0 \[[Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)\] further
incorporates tool-integrated reasoning into curriculum–executor
co-evolution, allowing the generated tasks to advance with the
executor’s capabilities. These methods demonstrate that task proposal
and task solving can form an autonomous feedback loop rather than
relying on a fixed, human-authored problem distribution.

Related frameworks extend self-evolution beyond standard mathematical
reasoning. Dr. Zero \[[Yue et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)\] co-evolves a
question proposer and a multi-turn search agent while reducing rollout
cost through hop-grouped relative optimization. SCOPE \[[Kwan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12)\] trains a Challenger and retrieval-based Solver on
open-ended, document-grounded tasks, using a frozen self-judge to
construct task-specific evaluation rubrics. CoEvolve \[[Yang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib9)\] extracts forgetting and uncertainty signals from
agent trajectories to guide subsequent tool-use task synthesis.
Agent-World \[[Dong et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)\], SEAD \[[Dai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib25)\], AgentEvolver \[[Zhai et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)\],
EvolveR \[[Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)\], and EvoFSM \[[Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib6)\] similarly evolve environments, curricula,
interaction experiences, memories, or agent workflows across tool use,
service dialogue, search, and general agentic settings. Collectively,
this literature establishes agent–data feedback as a promising basis for
autonomous and continual improvement.

The closest prior approaches adapt a proposer, teacher, or curriculum
policy according to an evolving solver, commonly emphasizing frontier
difficulty, weakness coverage, uncertainty, diversity, or verifier-based
task quality. Such adaptation is often implemented through round-wise
curriculum reconstruction, stage-wise policy optimization, or a fixed
generation module augmented with learner feedback. SynCo instead adopts
a more tightly coupled formulation: the same online interaction batch
produces rollout-level correctness rewards for the Reasoner and
task-level, interaction-grounded rewards for the Synthesizer, after
which both independently parameterized policies are updated within a
unified multi-agent training process. This setting also differs from
multi-agent post-co-training methods such as MAPoRL \[[Park et al.,
2025](#bib.bib53)\], which jointly optimize multiple agents for
collaborative response generation rather than training one policy to
construct another policy’s future learning experience. Beyond final
performance, we explicitly analyze whether synthesized tasks are
gradient-bearing, thereby distinguishing coarse difficulty and static
data quality from the realized optimization utility observed under the
current Reasoner.

## Appendix B Method

### B.1 Problem Formulation: Agentic Data Synthesis Co-Training

We consider a self-evolving learning system composed of two trainable
agents. The *Synthesizer* is parameterized by $`\theta_{S}`$ and defines
a data-synthesis policy $`\pi_{S}(\cdot;\theta_{S})`$, while the
*Reasoner* is parameterized by $`\theta_{R}`$ and defines a task-solving
policy $`\pi_{R}(\cdot;\theta_{R})`$. The two agents have fully
separated parameters and are optimized for different but mutually
dependent objectives. The Synthesizer controls which training
experiences are presented to the Reasoner, whereas the Reasoner’s
behavior on those experiences determines the task-level feedback
received by the Synthesizer.

At training iteration $`t`$, the system maintains an evolving synthesis
context $`c_{t}`$ that summarizes the current learning state.
Conceptually, $`c_{t}`$ captures the Reasoner’s recent task performance,
capability weaknesses, the coverage of the synthetic task distribution,
and feedback from previously rejected or redundant tasks. Given this
context, the Synthesizer samples a structured task

|     |                                                   |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       x_{t}\sim\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid c_{t};\theta_{S}^{t}),
       ```                                                |     | (12) |

where $`x_{t}`$ contains a problem specification together with the
information required to verify its validity and answer. Accordingly, the
training distribution at iteration $`t`$ is not externally fixed, but is
induced by the current synthesis policy and the current learner state:

|     |                                                          |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{D}_{t}=\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid c_{t};\theta_{S}^{t}).
       ```                                                       |     | (13) |

For each valid synthesized task $`x_{t}`$, the Reasoner produces a group
of $`K`$ independent solution rollouts,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y_{t}^{(k)}\sim\pi_{R}(\cdot\mid x_{t};\theta_{R}^{t}),\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.
``` |  | (14) |

Let $`a_{t}^{\star}`$ denote the verified reference answer associated
with $`x_{t}`$. An outcome verifier evaluates each rollout and returns

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{t}^{(k)}=\operatorname{Check}\left(y_{t}^{(k)},a_{t}^{\star}\right),
``` |  | (15) |

where $`z_{t}^{(k)}`$ indicates whether the rollout successfully solves
the task. The resulting interaction record is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{I}_{t}=\left(c_{t},x_{t},\left\{y_{t}^{(k)},z_{t}^{(k)}\right\}_{k=1}^{K}\right).
``` |  | (16) |

The same interaction $`\mathcal{I}_{t}`$ induces agent-specific rewards
for both policies. For the Reasoner, each rollout receives a
task-solving reward

|     |                                                                |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       r_{R,t}^{(k)}=R_{R}\left(x_{t},y_{t}^{(k)},z_{t}^{(k)}\right),
       ```                                                             |     | (17) |

which encourages correct and properly formatted solutions. For the
Synthesizer, the task receives a synthesis reward

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{S,t}=R_{S}\left(c_{t},x_{t},\left\{y_{t}^{(k)},z_{t}^{(k)}\right\}_{k=1}^{K}\right).
``` |  | (18) |

Unlike a static task-quality score, $`r_{S,t}`$ depends on how the
*current* Reasoner actually behaves on the synthesized task. It
therefore evaluates not only whether the task is valid and reliable, but
also whether it provides useful training experience for the present
Reasoner.

The two policies optimize their respective expected returns,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle J_{R}(\theta_{R})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x_{t}\sim\pi_{S},\,y_{t}^{(k)}\sim\pi_{R}}\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_{R,t}^{(k)}\right],`$ |  | (19) |
|  | $`\displaystyle J_{S}(\theta_{S})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x_{t}\sim\pi_{S},\,\{y_{t}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}\sim\pi_{R}}\left[r_{S,t}\right].`$ |  | (20) |

Although the agents receive distinct rewards and do not share
parameters, their optimization problems are intrinsically coupled. The
distribution underlying $`J_{R}`$ is determined by the Synthesizer
through
Eq. ([13](#A2.E13 "In B.1 Problem Formulation: Agentic Data Synthesis Co-Training ‣ Appendix B Method ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")),
while the reward underlying $`J_{S}`$ is determined partly by the
Reasoner’s rollout distribution. We jointly update the two policies from
the same online interaction process:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\theta_{R}^{t+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathcal{U}_{R}\left(\theta_{R}^{t},\mathcal{I}_{t},\{r_{R,t}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right),`$ |  | (21) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\theta_{S}^{t+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathcal{U}_{S}\left(\theta_{S}^{t},\mathcal{I}_{t},r_{S,t}\right),`$ |  | (22) |

where $`\mathcal{U}_{R}`$ and $`\mathcal{U}_{S}`$ denote the
corresponding group-relative policy optimization updates.

This formulation differs fundamentally from training a task model on an
independently synthesized dataset. Here, the Synthesizer directly
controls the Reasoner’s online learning distribution, and the Reasoner’s
realized behavior directly supervises the Synthesizer. Consequently,
data synthesis and task learning form a coupled multi-agent policy
optimization problem rather than two sequential training stages. The
following sections instantiate this formulation by describing how the
evolving Reasoner state conditions task synthesis, how shared task
interactions jointly optimize both agents, and how their updates
continuously reconstruct the subsequent training distribution.

### B.2 Reward and Verification Details

Each synthesized task is verified before entering Reasoner training. The
verifier checks schema completeness, problem well-posedness, answer
consistency, output validity, and redundancy with recently generated
tasks. We additionally apply an independent consensus check to filter
tasks whose reference answers are insufficiently supported by
independent solutions. Throughout training and evaluation, Reasoner
answers are judged using the same checker, which supports normalized
exact, numerical, symbolic, and set- or tuple-level equivalence.

For the Reasoner, each rollout receives a correctness-based reward: 1.0
for a correct answer in the prescribed format, 0.9 for a correct answer
recovered without that format, and 0 otherwise. For the Synthesizer, the
main experiments use an outcome-grounded gated reward:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{S,t}^{\mathrm{imm}}=G_{q}\!\left(r_{t}^{\mathrm{quality}}\right)G_{r}\!\left(r_{t}^{\mathrm{reliability}}\right)T(\mu_{t}),
``` |  | (23) |

where the quality and reliability gates follow

|     |                                                             |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       G(v)=\operatorname{clip}\left(\frac{v-0.5}{0.5},0,1\right).
       ```                                                          |     | (24) |

The task-quality score is a deterministic composite of verifier signals
measuring schema completeness, problem validity, answer consistency,
output format, and redundancy. The reliability score specifically
reflects the internal consistency between the Synthesizer-provided
reference solution and final answer. Both are computed using rule-based
checks rather than an LLM judge and primarily serve as feasibility
signals; exact verifier coefficients and thresholds are included in the
supplementary implementation.

Learner-dependent utility is determined by realized teachability. Given
the Reasoner’s empirical success rate
$`\mu_{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}z_{t}^{(k)}`$, we define

|     |                                                      |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       T(\mu_{t})=\begin{cases}2\mu_{t},&\mu_{t}\leq 0.5,\\
       2(1-\mu_{t}),&\mu_{t}>0.5.\end{cases}
       ```                                                   |     | (25) |

Teachability is therefore maximized when the Reasoner succeeds on half
of its rollouts and decreases toward zero as the rollout group becomes
uniformly correct or uniformly incorrect. The gated objective
consequently separates task feasibility from learner-relative utility:
quality and reliability constrain optimization toward trustworthy tasks,
while the current Reasoner’s realized behavior determines whether those
tasks provide informative group-relative feedback.

Tasks rejected by the verifier receive an immediate Synthesizer reward
of $`-0.5`$ and are excluded from Reasoner training. The training
framework additionally applies a constant 0.1 bonus to non-empty model
outputs. Novelty and diagnostic-alignment signals are logged for
analysis but do not directly contribute to the gated Synthesizer reward
used in the main experiments.

## Appendix C Experimental Details

### C.1 Benchmarks

We evaluate mathematical reasoning across eight benchmarks spanning
elementary word problems, competition mathematics, and higher-level
quantitative reasoning. GSM8K \[[Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib54)\]
contains grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic
reasoning, while SVAMP \[[Patel et al., 2021](#bib.bib55)\] stresses
robustness to variations in quantities and problem structure.
ASDiv \[[Miao et al., 2020](#bib.bib56)\] provides a more diverse
collection of arithmetic word problems with heterogeneous linguistic and
reasoning patterns. GSM-Hard \[[Gao et al., 2023](#bib.bib57)\]
increases the numerical difficulty of GSM8K-style problems while largely
preserving their underlying reasoning structure. MATH-500 \[[Hendrycks
et al., 2021](#bib.bib58), [Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib59)\] covers
competition-level algebra, geometry, number theory, counting,
probability, and related topics, requiring more involved symbolic and
multi-step reasoning. AIME24 and AIME25 each contain problems from the
corresponding American Invitational Mathematics Examination and provide
a challenging evaluation of competition-style reasoning with exact
answers. Minerva \[[Lewkowycz et al., 2022](#bib.bib60)\] contains
higher-level quantitative problems spanning advanced mathematics and
scientific reasoning. Together, these benchmarks cover a broad
difficulty range, from relatively saturated elementary reasoning to
substantially more challenging problems with greater learning headroom.
We use the standard test splits and report answer accuracy under the
same answer-extraction and verification pipeline for all methods.

### C.2 Baselines

We compare SynCo with three representative offline alternatives, an
iterative self-evolution baseline, and a matched frozen-Synthesizer
baseline. *Static-Pool GRPO* constructs a synthetic task pool before
training and optimizes only the Reasoner using GRPO \[[Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)\]. It isolates whether reinforcement learning over
fixed synthetic data can match an adaptively evolving training
distribution. *Offline-Augmented GRPO* constructs an offline task pool
through mathematical question rewriting and variation inspired by
MetaMath \[[Yu et al., 2023](#bib.bib16)\]. The Reasoner is subsequently
trained with GRPO while the augmented task distribution remains fixed.
*Rejection-Sampling SFT* samples Reasoner trajectories, retains those
with verified correct answers, and fine-tunes the model on the resulting
successful solutions. This baseline follows the
generate–filter–fine-tune self-training paradigm of ReST^(EM) \[[Singh
et al., 2023](#bib.bib61)\], without online policy optimization or
adaptive synthesis. *R-Zero* \[[Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)\]
co-evolves a Challenger and a Solver by iteratively generating tasks
near the Solver’s capability boundary and optimizing the two roles
through reinforcement learning. Unlike SynCo’s same-batch joint
optimization, R-Zero follows an alternating self-evolution process in
which task generation and solver improvement are updated across
successive stages. Finally, *SynCo (Frozen Synth.)* follows the same
online generation and Reasoner-training pipeline as SynCo, but keeps the
Synthesizer parameters fixed. This matched comparison isolates the
benefit of jointly optimizing the synthesis policy.

Further, we include two complementary groups of external baselines to
provide a broader comparison with existing synthetic-data approaches.

Released-checkpoint baselines. We first evaluate four publicly released
models that have undergone synthetic-data-driven agentic post-training.
AgenticQwen \[[Lyu et al., 2026](#bib.bib62)\] trains compact agentic
models through multi-round reinforcement learning with dual data
flywheels, where reasoning and agentic tasks are progressively
synthesized and increased in difficulty. EnvScaler \[[Song et al.,
2026](#bib.bib63)\] programmatically synthesizes executable
tool-interactive environments together with scenarios and rule-based
verification functions, and uses the resulting interaction data for SFT
and RL of Qwen3 models. AgentSkiller \[[Sun et al., 2026](#bib.bib64)\]
automatically constructs executable cross-domain environments and
synthesizes multi-turn interaction trajectories through structured
domain modeling, semantic cross-domain composition, and execution-based
validation. Klear-AgentForge \[[Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib65)\]
provides an open post-training pipeline that combines large-scale
synthetic-data SFT with subsequent multi-turn reinforcement learning for
general-purpose agentic capabilities. For these baselines, we directly
use the authors’ publicly released checkpoints without additional
training or adaptation, and evaluate them using exactly the same
mathematical evaluation protocol as SynCo.

Released synthetic-data baselines. We further compare against three
representative publicly released mathematical synthesis corpora while
controlling the downstream learner and optimization budget.
MetaMathQA \[[Yu et al., 2024](#bib.bib66)\] expands mathematical
supervision through question rephrasing and backward-reasoning-based
question generation, producing a large collection of augmented
mathematical problems. ScaleQuest-Math \[[Ding et al.,
2025](#bib.bib67)\] synthesizes mathematical questions from scratch
using lightweight question generators optimized through Question
Fine-Tuning and Question Preference Optimization, yielding a large-scale
corpus of synthetic problem–solution pairs.
OpenMathInstruct-2 \[[Toshniwal et al., 2025](#bib.bib68)\] constructs
massive open mathematical supervision through problem and solution
synthesis; for our comparison, we use its newly augmented synthetic
problems rather than unchanged original benchmark questions. For each
corpus, we sample exactly 2,940 unique synthetic problems, matching the
number of verified training tasks used by SynCo, and train the same
Qwen3 learner using the same GRPO implementation, rollout configuration,
optimizer settings, and total optimization budget as our controlled
static-data baseline.

### C.3 Implementation Details

We initialize the Synthesizer and the Reasoner as two independently
parameterized copies of Qwen3-8B, and additionally repeat the main
comparison with Qwen3-4B. Both agents are optimized using GRPO through
the UnityMAS-O \[[Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib69)\] training framework,
with vLLM serving as the rollout backend. Each training iteration
contains 32 synthesized tasks, and the Reasoner samples $`K=4`$
independent trajectories for every admitted task. We use an actor
learning rate of $`1\times 10^{-6}`$, a 10-step warm-up, weight decay of
0.1, and no KL penalty in the reward. During training, the Synthesizer
and Reasoner use temperatures of 1.0 and 0.9, respectively, with
$`p=0.95`$ nucleus sampling. The Qwen3-8B experiments are distributed
across two 8-GPU worker groups, one for each agent. The Qwen3-4B
experiments follow the same training protocol and hyperparameters except
for backbone-specific inference configurations. Each synthesized task is
verified for validity and answer reliability before entering Reasoner
training, with an additional consensus check used to filter unreliable
reference answers. For evaluation, we use temperature 0.6 and top-$`p`$
0.95, and apply the same answer checker to all methods, supporting
exact, numerical, symbolic, and set- or tuple-level equivalence. The
frozen-Synthesizer baseline uses the same backbone, Reasoner
optimization, rollout budget, verifier, and evaluation protocol, while
keeping the Synthesizer parameters fixed.

### C.4 Agent Prompt Templates

We provide the prompt templates used by the Synthesizer and the
Reasoner. At each synthesis iteration, the placeholders in the
Synthesizer user prompt are populated using the current synthetic-pool
statistics, the Reasoner’s recent capability diagnostics, and feedback
from rejected tasks. The Reasoner receives only the generated problem
statement; all pedagogical metadata, reference solutions, and
verification information are reserved for task validation and reward
computation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

When no interaction history is available, the context fields are
initialized with neutral descriptions indicating that no historical
pool, Reasoner diagnostics, or rejection records are yet available.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Shared prompt conventions.

Across the Synthesizer and Reasoner prompts, the system follows four
conventions: (1) the Synthesizer must generate exactly one original,
well-posed, and independently verifiable task; (2) the Synthesizer
output must be valid JSON following an explicitly specified schema; (3)
task generation is conditioned on synthetic-pool statistics, Reasoner
diagnostics, and rejection feedback when such interaction history is
available; and (4) the Reasoner receives only the generated problem
statement, while pedagogical metadata, reference solutions, and
verification information are reserved for task validation and reward
computation.

## Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis

### D.1 Generalization Across Model Scales

We further examine whether the benefits of synthesis co-training
generalize across model scales by repeating the main comparison with
Qwen3-4B. As shown in
Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ D.1 Generalization Across Model Scales ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning"),
the same progression observed with Qwen3-8B is reproduced: conditioning
a frozen Synthesizer on the evolving Reasoner raises the average
accuracy from 70.14% to 73.72%, while jointly optimizing the Synthesizer
further improves it to 75.20%. Thus, co-training contributes an
additional 1.48 percentage points over the matched frozen variant and
5.06 points over Vanilla. SynCo improves over its frozen counterpart on
seven of eight benchmarks and achieves the strongest overall average,
outperforming EnvScaler and AgentSkiller by 4.43 and 11.83 points,
respectively. While EnvScaler attains stronger results on AIME24 and
AIME25, SynCo performs more consistently across the broader benchmark
suite, achieving the best result on five benchmarks and ranking second
on the remaining three. The improvement is therefore not driven by a
single task family: gains appear across arithmetic reasoning, algebraic
and competition-style benchmarks, and Minerva, with only a small
regression on GSM-Hard. These results reproduce the main Qwen3-8B
finding at a smaller scale and show that the advantage of jointly
adapting the synthesis policy is robust to the Reasoner backbone rather
than being specific to a single model size.

### D.2 How Does the Synthesized Curriculum Evolve During Co-Training?

Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.2 How Does the Synthesized Curriculum Evolve During Co-Training? ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
provides a detailed decomposition of the 2,940 verified tasks collected
during co-training. We define a task as *gradient-bearing* when its
Reasoner rollout group receives non-identical rewards and therefore
produces non-zero group-relative advantages. Empirically, this criterion
is equivalent to $`0<\mathrm{SR}<1`$ for all verified task groups in our
collected training data. Only 475 tasks (16.2%) satisfy this condition,
compared with 994 (33.8%) that are uniformly incorrect and 1,471 (50.0%)
that are uniformly correct. Thus, the primary bottleneck is not
producing valid tasks, but continually placing them in the region where
the current Reasoner receives informative group-relative learning
signal.

The temporal evolution in
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 RQ2: How Does the Synthesized Curriculum Evolve During Co-Training? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
shows that this region becomes increasingly difficult to maintain.
Gradient-bearing tasks decrease from 31.3% in the earliest bucket to
9.5% in the final bucket, while the all-correct proportion rises from
34.4% to 59.9%. The shift is therefore driven primarily by tasks
becoming uniformly solvable as the Reasoner improves, rather than by an
increase in universally failed tasks. Meanwhile, task quality remains
high and novelty increases, showing that a curriculum can remain valid
and diverse while progressively losing optimization value. This
divergence highlights the non-stationarity of synthetic-data utility: a
task distribution that is useful for an earlier learner may gradually
fall behind its evolving capability frontier.

Panel (b) further separates static synthesis properties from
learner-dependent utility. Novelty is nearly uncorrelated with the
gradient-bearing indicator ($`r=-0.041`$), whereas outcome-grounded
teachability is strongly aligned with it ($`r=0.934`$), as expected from
its construction using realized rollout outcomes. Teachability is also
nearly uncorrelated with raw success rate ($`r=-0.028`$), indicating
that it does not simply favor easier or harder tasks but instead
emphasizes heterogeneous outcomes. Panel (c) reaches the same conclusion
from the Synthesizer’s ex-ante perspective: the *learnable*, *mid-band*,
and *hard/too hard* groups exhibit gradient-bearing rates of 16.8%,
16.0%, and 16.0%, respectively, all close to the 16.2% pool prevalence.
Thus, intended difficulty meaningfully shifts whether tasks are solved
or failed, but provides little information about whether they lie in the
optimization-relevant region. Together, these analyses show that
validity, novelty, and nominal difficulty characterize different
properties of synthetic data, but none substitutes for observing how the
current learner actually interacts with it.

|----|----|----|----|
|  Outcome Regime |  Criterion |  Number of Tasks |  Percentage |
|  All incorrect |  $`\mathrm{SR}=0`$ |  994 |  33.8% |
|  Gradient-bearing |  $`\mathbf{0<\mathrm{SR}<1}`$ |  475 |  16.2% |
|  All correct |  $`\mathrm{SR}=1`$ |  1,471 |  50.0% |
| (b) Synthesis Signals vs. Realized Utility |  |  |  |
|  Synthesis Signal |  Correlation Target |  Correlation |  Observed Alignment |
|  Teachability |  Gradient-bearing indicator |  +0.934 |  Strong positive |
|  Novelty |  Gradient-bearing indicator |  $`-0.041`$ |  Negligible |

|  Learnable |  630 |  16.8% |  83.2% |
|  Mid-band |  1,926 |  16.0% |  84.0% |
|  Hard / Too hard |  363 |  16.0% |  84.0% |
````
