### D.3 Attributing Gains to Capability Acquisition

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 RQ3: Where Do the Gains from Co-Training Arise? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
decomposes the terminal advantage of SynCo over SynCo (Frozen Synth.)
according to whether each evaluation example is initially solved by
Qwen3-8B. Both methods are evaluated at fixed terminal checkpoints,
avoiding benchmark-specific checkpoint selection. On the 2,560 initially
correct examples, the two variants remain close: SynCo retains 2,533
examples (98.95%), compared with 2,522 (98.52%) for the frozen variant,
yielding 11 additional retained solutions. The difference is
substantially larger on the 878 initially incorrect examples, where
SynCo solves 283 (32.23%) compared with 238 (27.11%) for Frozen. Thus,
the Learn subset contributes 45 of the 56 additional solved examples,
accounting for 80.4% of the overall advantage.

Figure [7](#A4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ D.3 Attributing Gains to Capability Acquisition ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
shows that this pattern holds consistently across all four benchmarks.
On GSM-Hard, the Learn subset contributes $`+21`$ of the $`+27`$ net
gain, compared with $`+6`$ from Retain. Similarly, Learn contributes
$`+9`$ of $`+11`$ on MATH-500, $`+11`$ of $`+13`$ on GSM8K, and $`+4`$
of $`+5`$ on SVAMP. In aggregate, co-training improves retention by only
$`+0.43`$ percentage points, from 98.52% to 98.95%, while improving
recovery on initially incorrect examples by $`+5.12`$ points, from
27.11% to 32.23%. The terminal advantage is therefore driven primarily
by increased success on examples outside the initial model’s competence,
rather than by preservation of already mastered behavior.

This decomposition complements the curriculum analysis in
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 RQ2: How Does the Synthesized Curriculum Evolve During Co-Training? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning").
Although only a minority of synthesized tasks produce non-degenerate
group-relative feedback, the resulting optimization translates
predominantly into newly solved evaluation examples rather than
additional retention of previously solved ones. This pattern appears
across all four benchmarks, including both relatively saturated datasets
and benchmarks with greater unresolved headroom. Together with the
aggregate improvements in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 RQ1: Does Co-Training Data Synthesis Improve Reasoning Performance? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning"),
these results support the role of adaptive synthesis in capability
acquisition: jointly evolving the synthesis policy helps the Reasoner
expand beyond its initial competence rather than merely consolidate
existing performance.

![Refer to caption](2610.11345v1/figures2/exp3_gain_attribution.png)

Figure 7: Attribution of SynCo’s terminal advantage over SynCo (Frozen
Synth.). *Retain* measures additional solved examples among those
initially solved by Qwen3-8B, whereas *Learn* measures gains on
initially incorrect examples. Across all four benchmarks, most of the
net improvement arises from the Learn subset, which contributes 45 of
the 56 additional solved examples (80.4%).

### D.4 Synthesis Signals and Realized Gradient Utility

Table [6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ D.4 Synthesis Signals and Realized Gradient Utility ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
examines how different synthesis signals relate to realized optimization
utility over the 2,940 verified tasks. Quality and reliability are
highly concentrated after verification, with means of 0.962 and 0.965,
respectively. This concentration is expected: both signals participate
in the gated synthesis reward and are also closely related to the
admissibility checks that remove malformed or unreliable tasks before
Reasoner training. Consequently, their weak correlations with the
gradient-bearing indicator should not be interpreted as evidence that
they are unnecessary; rather, once tasks pass verification, these
signals provide limited discrimination over which remaining tasks will
be useful for the current learner. Novelty exhibits substantially
greater variation but remains nearly uncorrelated with gradient
production ($`r=-0.041`$), showing that a task can be distinct from
previous generations without providing useful optimization signal.
Report alignment is similarly weakly associated with realized utility
and is used as a diagnostic context signal rather than as part of the
gated reward.

Outcome-grounded teachability behaves fundamentally differently. Its
correlation with the gradient-bearing indicator reaches $`r=0.934`$,
while its correlation with raw Reasoner success rate is only
$`r=-0.028`$. Thus, teachability does not simply favor easier or harder
tasks; it identifies tasks whose rollout groups contain heterogeneous
outcomes and therefore provide non-degenerate group-relative feedback.
This distinction is central to the reward design of SynCo: quality and
reliability constrain optimization toward trustworthy tasks, while
realized Reasoner behavior determines which of those tasks are useful
for learning.

The reranking analysis in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 RQ4: Which Synthesis Signals Align with Gradient-Bearing Tasks? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
makes this separation explicit. Selecting the top quartile according to
the actual SynCo gated reward raises the gradient-bearing rate from the
pool prevalence of 16.2% to 62.3%, a $`3.9\times`$ enrichment. Outcome
teachability alone reaches 64.6% ($`4.0\times`$), whereas quality-only
and novelty-only rankings yield only 12.8% and 12.0%, respectively. The
small difference between teachability alone and the full gated reward
reflects their different roles: teachability identifies outcome-level
learning utility, while the quality and reliability gates prevent
optimization from favoring informative but invalid or unreliable tasks.
Hence, the objective is not designed to maximize gradient yield in
isolation, but to identify useful learning experiences within a feasible
synthesis space.

| Synthesis Signal | Mean | Std. |  Corr. with Gradient-Bearing |  Role |  Interpretation within Verified Pool |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Quality | 0.962 | 0.030 | $`+0.060`$ |  Reward gate |  Nearly saturated after verification, with limited discrimination among valid tasks. |
| Reliability | 0.965 | 0.096 | $`+0.105`$ |  Reward gate |  Ensures answer consistency and reliability, but weakly predicts realized gradient utility. |
| Report alignment | 0.999 | 0.011 | $`-0.021`$ |  Diagnostic |  Nearly constant in the collected pool and weakly associated with realized utility. |
| Novelty | 0.703 | 0.175 | $`-0.041`$ |  Diagnostic |  Varies substantially across tasks but does not identify gradient-bearing interactions. |
| Teachability | 0.102 | 0.249 | $`+0.934`$ |  Outcome utility |  Strongly aligned with whether the task produces non-degenerate group-relative feedback. |

reward used by SynCo, whereas novelty and report alignment are recorded
as diagnostic signals. Correlation is measured against the binary

### D.5 Why Ex-Ante Difficulty Does Not Predict Gradient Utility

Table [7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ D.4 Synthesis Signals and Realized Gradient Utility ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
compares the Synthesizer’s ex-ante difficulty estimates with the
outcomes realized by the current Reasoner. The estimates exhibit
meaningful coarse calibration: tasks labeled *learnable* have an average
success rate of 0.625, whereas those labeled *hard/too hard* average
0.484. Consistently, the proportion of uniformly correct tasks decreases
from 53.0% to 39.9%, while the uniformly incorrect proportion increases
from 30.2% to 44.1%. The Synthesizer therefore captures the broad
direction of task difficulty and can shift generation from easier toward
harder regions of the task space.

However, calibration of average difficulty does not imply calibration of
optimization utility. The gradient-bearing rates remain nearly unchanged
at 16.8%, 16.0%, and 16.0% for the *learnable*, *mid-band*, and
*hard/too hard* groups, respectively, all close to the 16.2% pool
prevalence. Increasing nominal difficulty therefore primarily transfers
probability mass from uniformly correct to uniformly incorrect outcomes
rather than increasing the likelihood of mixed rollout groups. This
distinction is important under group-relative optimization: a task can
become substantially harder while remaining equally uninformative if all
sampled trajectories still receive the same outcome. Ex-ante difficulty
and realized gradient utility are therefore related but fundamentally
different quantities.

Panel (b) quantifies this gap directly. Treating the Synthesizer’s
*learnable* label as a binary predictor of gradient-bearing tasks yields
a correlation of only $`0.009`$, with 16.8% precision and 22.3% recall.
Its precision is essentially identical to the underlying pool
prevalence, indicating that the label provides almost no enrichment for
optimization-relevant tasks. Moreover, most gradient-bearing tasks fall
outside the *learnable* category, showing that useful interactions
cannot be isolated reliably through self-estimated difficulty alone. The
difficulty label is therefore better interpreted as a generation intent
than as a prediction of downstream learning value.

By contrast, outcome-grounded teachability is computed after observing
the Reasoner’s rollouts and is strongly aligned with the
gradient-bearing indicator ($`r=0.934`$) by construction. Its role is
consequently different from ex-ante difficulty: the former identifies
realized learning utility, whereas the latter only guides where in the
task space synthesis should occur before interaction. Together with
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 RQ4: Which Synthesis Signals Align with Gradient-Bearing Tasks? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning"),
this analysis explains why SynCo closes the loop between generation and
learner feedback. Static task attributes and self-estimated difficulty
can steer exploration, but determining whether a task actually provides
non-degenerate learning signal requires observing the current Reasoner’s
behavior.

statistics are reported as secondary references because the two runs
were executed independently. Productive-task statistics are computed
over steps 13–70, the interval with valid logging for both variants.
Task-generation, verification, and rollout computation are included in
the reported runtime.

Table 8: Detailed efficiency analysis of online Synthesizer–Reasoner
co-training. Panel (a) compares per-step training cost, Panel (b)
reports productive-task yield over the matched logging window, and Panel
(c) summarizes task generation and verification during the 100-step
SynCo run.

### D.6 Training Efficiency, Gradient Utilization, and Data Production

Table [8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ D.5 Why Ex-Ante Difficulty Does Not Predict Gradient Utility ‣ Appendix D Extended Experimental Analysis ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning")
provides a detailed efficiency analysis of SynCo and its
frozen-Synthesizer counterpart. As shown in Panel (a), jointly
optimizing the Synthesizer introduces little additional per-step
computation. The mean synchronized update times are 45.1 s for SynCo and
45.8 s for Frozen, with corresponding median update times of 44.6 s and
45.0 s. Median end-to-end step times are likewise comparable at 343.5 s
and 341.6 s. Because the runs were executed independently, these small
wall-clock differences should be interpreted as comparable computational
profiles rather than evidence that either variant is intrinsically
faster. The key result is that enabling Synthesizer optimization does
not materially increase the cost of the otherwise matched online
training pipeline.

Panel (b) examines how this comparable computation is converted into
useful training signal over the matched logging window. The
productive-task rate increases from 13.7% under Frozen to 14.5% with
SynCo, corresponding to 4.38 versus 4.64 productive tasks per batch of
32. The increase is modest, but it is obtained without increasing the
rollout budget or Reasoner optimization cost. This suggests that
adapting the synthesis policy improves the allocation of a fixed
interaction budget: rather than generating more experience, SynCo
slightly increases the frequency with which generated tasks fall into
regions that provide non-degenerate group-relative feedback. This
complements the optimization dynamics in
Section [4.7](#S4.SS7 "4.7 RQ7: Does SynCo Better Match the Learner’s Capability Boundary? ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning"),
where the same training process produces a progressively stronger
Reasoner trajectory.

Panel (c) summarizes the resulting online data-production process.
Across 100 training steps, SynCo generates 3,200 task candidates, of
which 2,940 pass verification, yielding a 91.9% acceptance rate. The
resulting curriculum is generated and verified within the training loop
without human annotation or external LLM API calls. These numbers should
not be interpreted as zero synthesis cost: generation, verification, and
Reasoner rollouts are already included in the measured runtime. Rather,
they show that the evolving training distribution is constructed
internally as part of the same optimization process, without requiring a
separate data-generation stage.
